html:
An Australian silent film of 1906 about the bushranger Ned Kelly and his gang, often called the world's first feature length narrative film. It ran for over an hour, longer than any story film made before it.

It was made in and around Melbourne by the Tait brothers, theatre showmen, and directed by Charles Tait. It told the story of the Kelly gang, outlaws hanged or killed in 1880, and ended with Ned Kelly in his homemade iron armour at the siege of Glenrowan. It opened at the Athenaeum Hall in Melbourne on 26 December 1906, toured Australia and New Zealand, and was shown in Britain. Some authorities worried that such films made heroes of criminals, and bushranger films were later banned in some states.

Only about 17 minutes of the film survive, pieced together from fragments found over the years. In 2007 it was added to UNESCO's Memory of the World Register. It shows how early Australia took to cinema, years before Hollywood made features. See Australia.
